utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, if you're ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I can return to completing the submissions on the Croatian crime base. Evidence will be led to show the limited role expected and played by the DB. This evidence will contradict the ridiculous theory advanced through Babic and others that allege that Mr. Stanisic not only managed to take over the Serbian MUP but also subverted the whole of the SAO Krajina leadership and military machine and bent them to his will. It is alleged that there was a so-called parallel structure with Milosevic at the head, followed by Stanisic, with the TO of Krajina, the volunteer units, and Martic's Police or the militia of Krajina along with certain presidents of the municipalities. That case rests upon the fiction that in 1991 onwards, Mr. Stanisic had untrammeled power, that he was Mr. Milosevic's right-hand man. As stated at paragraph 45 of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, Mr. -- sorry, Minister Sokolovic was just a figurehead and Mr. Stanisic was the de facto minister of the interior. However, as the Defence case will show, that alleged state of affairs appears to have escaped everyone's notice at that time. Bogdanovic was the minister of interior of Serbia until June 1991. He, like his successor Sokolovic, was a high-ranking functionary in the Communist Party and thereafter in Milosevic's SPS party. Stanisic was not even a member of either party. When he became chief of the service, in order to prevent the service from becoming a political tool, he actively discouraged anyone from joining any political party. Mr. Stanisic was subject to a politically motivated investigation in 1991. Bogdanovic and Junackovic tried to remove him. It was only his professionalism and respect from within the service that may have saved him. Your Honours will recall P630, an intercepted telephone conversation between Karadzic and Kertes on the 24th of June, 1991. Kertes claimed to Karadzic that Jovica had been given carte blanche, and the Prosecution allege, that is carte blanche to supply weapons to Bosnia. The Defence case will demonstrate that that is not correct, but in any event, as the Defence will advance, there could not conceivably have been a criminal purpose in existence in Bosnia in June of 1991, but the point I'd make at this stage is this: Kertes was right about one thing. Jovica's hands were tied and he was driving -- that is Junackovic was driving Mr. Stanisic crazy. It's a reference to Mr. Stanisic being subject to an internal investigative commission, politically motivated by members of Milosevic's political party. It doesn't make sense, we submit, to suggest that Stanisic was the most powerful man in the MUP and yet his hands were tied by Junackovic. The Supreme Defence Council minutes from the FRY during 1992 make it crystal clear that Mr. Stanisic, firstly, did not take part in any of that decision-making. Regular attendees of the Supreme Defence Council were members of the federal administration. Various leaders of the former Yugoslavia, as well as senior members of the military. The Supreme Defence Council minutes show the Serbian and Montenegrin contribution to the wars in Croatia and Bosnia. They show that the decisions were primarily dictated from this decision-making body. I shall return to these minutes later on, but the Serbian MUP was not invited. Mr. Sokolovic attended once on the 7th of August, 1992. From 1992 through to the end of 1995, Mr. Stanisic, this omnipresent and omnipotent chief, is mentioned once in the context of making an ordinary arrest. His service barely warrants a mention. We have placed these minutes on our exhibit list. It's an eloquent demonstration of the inaccuracy of the Prosecution case against Mr. Stanisic and the DB that the Prosecution did not do the same. As the Defence case will show, all the documentary evidence from Supreme Defence Council minutes to the 108 -- 88th session of the Presidency, the SFRY, on the 25th of February, 1992, to the various personal diaries that have emerged, all fail to place Stanisic at the centre of the action. The Prosecution case impliedly accepts this. That is why they allege he was a channel of communication. It means that he was not a decision-maker. Of course, as the various exhibits we will adduce will show, the political and military leadership required no channel of communication. There are tens and tens of intercepts reflecting direct contacts between the politicians and the military. Given the role and importance that is sought to be attributed to Mr. Stanisic, it is instructive how little he appears. Mr. Milosevic required no channel of communication to speak to Karadzic. As the intercepts will show, at times he was on the phone directly with him almost every day. Slide 21: The Mladic diaries are a little interesting. As Prosecution Exhibit 2529 shows, on the 2nd of July, 1993, Mladic has a meeting with Sainovic, Badza, Karadzic, Krajisnik, Stanisic and others. Sainovic introduces Stanisic and Badza as the men who carry out things, an interesting description that the Prosecution rely upon as an indication of Mr. Stanisic's importance. However, the more interesting fact has been obscured. The diaries start on the 29th of June, 1991, just before Mladic became a colonel and Chief of Staff of the 9th Corps of the JNA in Knin, and before he moved to being the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS on the 12th of May, 1992. The Stanisic that appears before this -- before this 2nd of July, 1993, meeting is Mico Stanisic, and Your Honours can see the entries which relate to him. Even if that is disputed by the Prosecution, the entries indicate a Stanisic who is relatively unimportant. The whole war had raged in Croatia in 1991 and in Bosnia in 1992, and the first accused, Milosevic's right-hand man, doesn't appear in Mladic's diaries. Witnesses DST-34, 62, 31, and 43 - our fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh witnesses - all occupied significant roles within the Krajina either on a permanent or temporary basis. Their political or professional roles meant that they were close to the federal state or the RSK leadership, including Martic and Babic. They did not see or hear of Stanisic's involvement with weapon supplies, the Krajina government, with Dragan, with Golubic, with the police of the Krajina, or their training. They, unlike certain prosecution witnesses, like Mr. Lazarevic, did not request or receive relocation packages to comfortable countries overseas. They have no reason to lie to assist Mr. Stanisic. Witnesses DST-35, 44, 63, and 30 will confirm that the same is true in the SBWS. 35, 44, and 63 were all busy professionals working along the border of Serbia with Croatia. Their jobs meant they were operating along the border between Serbia and the SBWS or inside SBWS itself. The witnesses will confirm the role of the Vojvodina SUP and the Serbian MUP in trying to protect the border, prevent the illegal transport of weapons from Serbia into Croatia and back into Serbia. The witnesses will confirm their role in setting up police stations within the SBWS. It's our submission that these police forces were largely a force for good, preventing crimes and bringing law and order in a region in desperate need of security. DST-35 will describe how this was undermined by the minister of the interior, Bogdanovic, who for personal reasons made sure that Arkan could travel freely with weapons into the SBWS region. DST-44 will describe the friendship between his superior Badza and Arkan. That friendship prevented other more responsible authorities from taking restraining action. It is Badza, if he was alive, and Bogdanovic who should be sitting where Mr. Stanisic is. It is them who provided Arkan and others with support. DST-44 will confirm the collaboration between the Vojvodina SUP, the Serbian DB, and the Serbian public security in action Srem designed to protect non-Serbs along the border. All these witnesses will confirm that the DB's role was limited to gathering intelligence. The Serbian DB did not even assist in the establishment of the RSK DB in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, your speed of speech is slowly going up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I'm just becoming conscious of the time, but I'll slow it down, Your Honour. The Prosecution cannot prove, we submit, and the Defence case will show that Stanisic played a role in the formation and sustenance of the RSK. In the absence of convincing evidence, they fall back on the mythology of the Red Berets that allegedly began with Mr. Stanisic taking Captain Dragan to Knin. The Defence case will refute that allegation. It is based on rumour, speculation, and Captain Dragan's boastful ways. If we can return for a moment to P1050, the diary of Glisic, the secretary to General Simovic, the Ministry of Defence, written sometime in 1992. As the evidence will show, there is a theme that's developed through the documents. Once again -- once again, Mr. Stanisic does not get star billing. On the contrary, he doesn't even make an appearance in Simovic's office, and he's not even discussed. Your Honours will be invited to read the various portions, they can be found at 1D2616 to 1D2627. The entries read like a who's who of the moment, from Milosevic, Babic, Hadzic, Arkan, Kertes, General Kadijevic, General Adzic, Admiral Brovet, retired General Pekic, and of course the infamous Dragan. The only man of apparent significance who does not make an appearance is Mr. Stanisic. The Prosecution make much of P992, slide 25 -- I beg your pardon, slide 33. Dragan, of course, claimed in a letter that was sent to the command of the TO on the 8th of November, 1991, that he had an obligation towards the state security of the Republic of Serbia and his activities had to be fully in accordance with that service. Putting aside the vagueness of that claim, as with all Dragan's and prosecutorial claims, we invite Your Honours to put it to the test. As the exhibit shows, P992, Captain Dragan was disgruntled about Simovic's request that he become an ordinary captain of the TO. At the time he wrote the letter, he was famous throughout Serbia, far beyond his actual achievements. He wanted to be the commander of a new Serbian Army. As the Defence evidence will show, he thought that by claiming obligations towards the state security that Simovic -- I've just been helpfully reminded. It's slide 25 we're looking at, beg your pardon. He wanted to be the commander of a new Serbian Army. He thought that by claiming obligations towards the state security, Simovic would allow that to happen. Simovic having refused, Dragan launched a virulent press campaign against Simovic and the Ministry of Defence, making all sorts of outlandish claims about the DB. Your Honours will see from slide 26 another outlandish claim by Dragan concerning the Serbian Special Police forces. The Defence case will explain the Red Beret story. The evidence will strip away the mythology. We agree that the story starts with Dragan and the selection of certain recruits from those who trained at Golubic. The unit consisted of instructors and some recruits who had already been trained at Golubic. The name of the group was the Knindzas. The unit under the command of Captain Dragan in autumn of 1991 engaged in military operations, mostly in the direction of the Plitvice lakes. The Knindzas were operating under Martic, because the Knindzas were part of the police. Second in command was Dragan. The third in command was Crnogorac. They participated in the operation in Plitvice. The goal of the operation was to push the Croatian forces out. Mr. Simatovic was not in command of the unit. They received orders from Martic. They were not part of the DB, as the Mladic diaries we referred to earlier suggest. They were indistinguishable from the RSK police, because they were the RSK police. At some point in time in autumn of 1991, the Knindzas were ordered to assist the JNA in capturing Ilok. They based themselves in Fruska Gora. That 25- to 30-strong group included Crnogorac and Raja Bozovic. As the Defence evidence will show, principally through DST-42, it was around this time that Mr. Stanisic became involved with the group. He negotiated to use some of the Knindzas to assist with Serbian state security duties. Ilok is just a few kilometres distance from Pajzos where an intelligence outpost of the DB service was located. It consisted of an electronic surveillance installation and men from the Knindzas were used to secure it. Members of this security detail did not take part in any military operations on behalf of the Serbian DB. Your Honours may recall the evidence of Prosecution witness JF-031, who recalled Mr. Stanisic visiting Fruska Gora in October of 1991 or thereabouts. Mr. Stanisic visited with his young son who was clutching a magazine with the Knindzas on the front. The Knindzas were famous, and his son wanted to see this now famous group. Had Fruska Gora been a proper military base, would Stanisic have brought his young son? Stanisic had in mind that this group might be useful to the state security of Serbia for a limited purpose. As was confirmed by JF-031, Stanisic emphasised that the men to be used for Pajzos were not to be used for military operations. Panic was persuaded that the men should not be used for operations in Vukovar. We rely upon that evidence. It is a colourful demonstration of Mr. Stanisic's intent. Whilst the JNA, the TO, volunteers including Arkan, were hell bent on destroying Vukovar, Stanisic refused to be involved or to allow himself to be drawn into that war. A short while later, a group of men including Bozovic entered Pajzos and began guarding it on behalf of the Serbian MUP. They remained part of the -- they remained part of the RSK police and were commanded by Martic. They were on loan to the DB of Serbia for that and only that task. The remainder of the Knindzas were assigned by Martic elsewhere and had nothing to do with the Serbian DB. It is perhaps possible that had Mr. Stanisic's role with these men ended there with the subcontracting of a limited number for this limited purpose, he may not have found himself as an accused in this trial. However, in early 1992, a terrorist group from Croatia infiltrated into Serbia and had to be hunted down and captured in the Serbian town of Apatin. Mr. Stanisic came with Badza it assess how to handle the situation. The SAJ, the public security anti-terrorist unit, was temporarily out of action. A decision was made to use a small group of the Knindzas, including Raja Bozovic to catch these terrorists who were eventually handed over in a prisoner exchange to the Croatians. Mr. Simatovic noted this fact in his Kula speech. He dated that this was one of the most important tasks undertaken by the Serbian special unit, capturing the terrorists from Apatin. He got the date wrong and placed that occurrence in 1993, but nonetheless, it's a curious aspect of his speech that despite co-ordinating 5.000 men in Krajina, setting up 26 training camps, supervising thousands of flights transporting essential military and humanitarian equipment, active participation in six operations in Croatia and Bosnia, Mr. Simatovic should describe the capture of 20 or so terrorists as one of the main successes of the special unit of the DB. It was one of the most important, because the remainder was just not true. Following that operation, part of that group captured terrorists from Apatin misbehaved and had a conflict with the police in Apatin. One of them was assaulted by Bozovic. Stanisic ordered that the group should no longer be used by the DB, and Bozovic was sent a clear message he was no longer welcome in Serbia. Around this time, in February 1992, the UN forces had moved into Croatia pursuant to the Vance Peace Plan. The men who had been members of the Knindzas were no longer together as one group. There were members in Knin, members in Korenica. Zika Crnogorac went to Slavonia and turned up in Brcko. Captain Dragan had some of his other men in SAO Baranja. These were not offshoots of the DB's special unit but ex-members of the Knindzas operating as professional volunteers. The Defence will show that Mr. Stanisic had nothing to do with dispatching these men to Bosnia or anywhere else. The allegation is based on the theory of a case that once again implies a level of authority and planning that simply wasn't there. There is powerful evidence, and we rely upon it and we'll corroborate it, that Mr. Stanisic had nothing to do with dispatching Bozovic to Bosnia. As Exhibit 392, Mladic's diary, clearly shows, Bozovic, a professional volunteer, received a request from the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps in Bosnia, General Talic, to report to the Doboj centre. The chief of the centre was Andrija Bijocevic. 15 or 20 men were transferred with Bozovic. In our submission the Mladic diary 392 is proof positive that Mr. Stanisic did not arrange for Bozovic to go to Doboj. He didn't arrange for Bozovic. He didn't arrange for any of the men to go anywhere. That is the story of the genesis of the Red Berets which will be outlined in the Defence case. It's the story of men who informed a group that became famous. Their fame was enhanced by claims of their connections to the DB. The journalists and the Prosecution did the rest. As DST-40 will confirm, there existed a Serbian MUP decision dated the 4th of August, 1993, to form an anti-terrorist unit. The evidence will clearly show that this was the formation of a new unit. It required planning and organisation. It wouldn't have been needed if the Prosecution theory is correct. DST-40 will testify to the efforts made to create this unit. He will confirm and elaborate that the formation of such a unit is a difficult endeavour. It takes years to set up a professional unit. DST-40 will confirm the DB's committed attempts to employ appropriate people. The concept of reserve forces is important in this case. The MUP Serbia was legally entitled, in fact obligated, to employ reserve forces when they were needed to prevent activities aimed at endangering the security of the country. The Defence case will show that Mr. Stanisic had no role in employing or paying reserve forces. He had no role in the employment of persons who the Prosecution claim to be key members of the special unit of the Serbian DB. That certain undesirable men may have found their way onto the list of reserve forces, that is the temporary forces, is unsurprising in the chaos of war. However, it has nothing to do with Mr. Stanisic, in the same way that the employment of temporary staff in this court has nothing to do with the President of the ICTY. Slide number 28 shows the type of employment decisions that Mr. Stanisic made. The Defence case will show that these themselves were barely decisions. There was a commission at the centre of the 8th administration, the administration which dealt with logistics and supplies. The commission made the selection of employees, and Mr. Stanisic would sign those decisions. In the absence of a good obvious reason not to, Mr. Stanisic was effectively rubber-stamping other decisions. That members of the Knindzas or those they associated with, or reserve forces, would claim to be members of the DB is again unsurprising. Find me a bar in the world full of men with military experience, and I will find you a man who claims to have been a man of special forces. Find me a man who fought alongside any of the ex-Knindzas during the Balkans war, and I will find you a member of the Red Berets. It's a convenient prosecutorial theory, but it's a poor way we submit to attribute individual culpability for international crimes. Part three of the Defence case will deal with the alleged contribution of the accused to the Bosnia and Herzegovina crime base. It will set out to demonstrate three central propositions: First, that there is absolutely no reliable evidence that supports the existence of a criminal purpose in Bosnia before April of 1992. Second, that had the Serbian political or military authorities from Serbia participated in any criminal purpose after that date, which is doubtful, they had most certainly withdrawn from it by late 1993 at the latest. The Defence will show that the Serbian military and political authorities withdrew any meaningful co-operation from the Bosnian Serb leadership at around this time. There was no shared concerted action in furtherance of any criminal purpose. The third part of this section of the Defence will show that Mr. Stanisic did not at any time share any criminal purpose, nor did he contribute in any way. Dealing with the first point, there was no criminal purpose in Bosnia and no evidence to suggest otherwise until at least April 1992. The Prosecution case establishes that in late August 1991, the SDS leadership within Bosnia began to consider the creation of separate Serb territory with a view to enabling Serbs to remain in Yugoslavia. This plan envisaged the institution of separate structures, including the police and the military and the political arenas. The Prosecution case also establishes that on the 19th or 20th of December, 1991, the document which became known as the implementing instructions for Variant A and B was introduced by Karadzic to a meeting of high-level SDS representatives. On the 16th Republika Srpska Assembly session, Karadzic outlined the Bosnian Serb six strategic objectives. I hope Your Honours will forgive me from reading a section of the Krajisnik judgement which -- upon which we will rely, paragraphs 995 and 996: "It would be incorrect to place these goals on a pedestal ... for in the final analysis they are anodyne statements, severing as official state policy and even qualifying for publication in the Bosnian Serb Republic's 'Official Gazette.' If one is inclined to find in them insidious hidden meanings it's because of the context and the events that followed, and an anachronistic reading of the May goals is not only inadvisable, it misses the point. "Much more important in relation to actual policy was the feedback loop of co-ordination and support that existed between Bosnian Serb forces on the ground and the central leadership. Takeovers, killings, detention, abuse, expulsions ..." and so on, "had begun in the territories ... before the pronouncement of the strategic goals on the 12th of May, 1992. These incidents were launched in early ... 1992 ..." The Defence will rely upon this to assert that there could not have been any shared criminal purpose until this time. A plurality of persons acting in concert in pursuit of a common purpose, whilst we do not accept that the Serbian political and military leadership were part of any plurality acting in pursuit of any criminal purpose within Bosnia, the Defence will demonstrate that following the Bosnian Serbs' rejection of peace endeavours, any co-operation or collaboration between the two became minimal. It became, from the Serbian -- from Serbia proper, intended only to prevent war and a burgeoning refugee crisis in Serbia. The framework of the defence we shall present will rest on the discussions and decisions that took place in the Supreme Defence Council of the remnants of the SFRY. The disenchantment with the extremists from the Bosnian Serb leadership began in 1992, and by late 1994, co-operation that might imply a shared criminal goal and criminal intent had long since ceased. Slide 30 is an excerpt from the Supreme Defence Council minutes in June of 1993. It is clear from reading these minutes that Serbian authorities, the leadership who were part of the Supreme Defence Council, had enough. There was still some assistance as the Supreme Defence Council minutes reflect. However, this did not last long. As slide 31 demonstrates, and of course we invite Your Honours to read the whole of the minutes, the FRY decided to sever relationships with its -- leadership of VRS. It reiterated that it should wield influence on the Republika Srpska because peace was in its common and most important national and state interests. It recognised that if Banja Luka was bombed, there would be a hundred thousand refugees flooding into Serbia. Slide 32 and 33 are more of the same. This nation, Serbia, shall not be slaughtered because of three hot-heads from Pale. By the 27th of September, 1994, the time of the 25th Session, the Supreme Defence Council most certainly had had enough. However, the decisions to withdraw aid and assistance were not straightforward. The security of the Bosnian Serbs was also a matter of security within Serbia. This is discussed at length in the Supreme Defence Council minutes. Slide 34 reflects on the 20 -- I beg your pardon. On the 2nd of November, 1994, the -- the Supreme Defence Council recognised the reality. They recognised that whilst not wanting to assist with the Bosnian Serbs' territorial objectives, there was a need to prevent the war flooding into Serbia. There was a need to return refugees to the Bihac region. These were the discussions which were the basis for Pauk. These were the discussions which were the basis for Mr. Stanisic's involvement in Pauk. Slide 35, of huge relevance, we submit, for the Prosecution case in 1995. The Supreme Defence Council recognised a real threat if the Bosnian Serbs were defeated. The security of Serbia was threatened. Refugees and the crisis that would be caused were at the forefront of the participants' minds. The aforementioned Supreme Defence Council minutes and decisions will be the framework of the Defence case relating to the Bosnian crime base. The Defence evidence will show that there can be no doubt that any shared criminal purpose had ended long before 1995. The assistance offered in late 1994 onwards by Mr. Stanisic to Operation Pauk was not motivated by any criminal intent but a genuine desire to bring the leadership of the RSK to the peace table and to solve a genuine refugee crisis in Bihac and to prevent a larger one in Serbia. The operations in Trnovo and the operations in Banja Luka must be seen in this light. That is why the Prosecution have struggled to explain the relevance of Pauk to their joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecution's joint criminal enterprise fails to distinguish lawful action in pursuant of lawful objectives and war in pursuant of crime. Mr. Stanisic, we submit, did not contribute to the Bosnian crime base. The Defence will show that the accused did not contribute in any way to the criminal purpose, if one existed, in Bosnia. As the Defence will show, there is simply no reliable evidence. Mr. Mladic's crude attempt to implicate Mr. Stanisic through a set of doctored diaries will be exposed. The Bosnian Serb MUP arose from an enactment on the 28th of February, 1992, the Bosnian Serb Law on Internal Affairs. The Bosnian Serb MUP was to handle security affairs on behalf of the government. We accept that in the early days the Bosnian Serb MUP co-ordinated with and was helped by the Republic of Serbia. Reports prepared by the federal State Security Services in March 1992 confirm formal co-operation between the federal SUP in Belgrade and the Bosnian SUP police. The Defence case will prove that this co-ordination plan did not involve the Serbian DB. It is powerful proof of Mr. Stanisic's state of mind that his service did not assist the Bosnian MUP or DB. This is borne out by the Mladic diaries, and even with the attempt to implicate Mr. Stanisic, they bear witness to Mr. Stanisic's failure to assist. As I've already outlined earlier, it is true that Stanisic introduced a meeting with Mladic on the 13th of December, 1993, and stated: "It is because of your initiative we are meeting to improve your operational and tactical position and see about helping Serbia," but it is also true that Stanisic did not say another word at that meeting, according to Mladic. He was, in that instance, going through a formality, merely introducing the meeting. The Defence will show that neither he nor his service assisted the Bosnian Serbs. The Defence case will show that the assistance to the Bosnian Serbs came from other quarters. Slides 36 to 48 show a reflection and a representative selection of where that assistance came from. These exhibits show where that assistance came from. Slide 48, Prosecution 65 ter 2351, a request sent to Stanisic from the Republika Srpska MUP, 12th of May, 1995: "Could your technical service please repair and service a mobile 400-watt shortwave communication centre, generate a unit and a vehicle. Could you please also reconsider our earlier request for the necessary technical equipment." That, in June 1995 when Mr. Stanisic was supposed to be at the height of his powers, is how the Republika Srpska MUP regards Mr. Stanisic. Your Honours will note the "request to reconsider our earlier request." Mr. Stanisic did not form any co-operative relationship with the Bosnian DB. That is why largely absent from the Mladic diaries. There was an open conflict between his service and the Bosnian service. Mr. Stanisic did not like General Mladic as Mr. Stanisic had declined to become involved with Vukovar in late 1991. He wanted no part in attacks on safe areas or the disgraceful bombing of civilian areas such as those in Sarajevo and elsewhere. This animosity turned to open conflict in June of 1995, when Mr. Stanisic negotiated the release of the UNPROFOR hostages. It was plain to Mr. Stanisic that he was not negotiating with a rational man. Unfortunately but predictably, that lack of reason has not been removed over the last 15 years. Despite fact that Mladic had ample opportunity and every reason to do so over the last 15 years to doctor his account, the Prosecution in this case proffer them without reservation as truth. It will be interesting to see if that's the position adopted during the prosecution of Mladic. It is plain on their face, we submit, and the Defence case will show through detailed evidence that they are self-serving when implicating others. The massacres in Srebrenica appear not to have occurred in the world outlined by Mr. Mladic. The Defence case will show that the entries implicating Stanisic barely make sense and will not be corroborated. If I can return to the 2nd of July, 1993, meeting where Stanisic is alleged to have said: "The majority of what we need should be issued via the MUP of Serbia. The centres should be Pale, Herzegovina, and Talic." There is no evidence that the Serbian MUP set up centres in these locations. There's no evidence that Talic is even a location but might be a reference to General Talic. It is, however, quite telling, and the Defence case will elaborate on this point, that at the end of the meeting, Mladic takes only Sainovic's number, telephone number. Of course, when one reads the Supreme Defence Council minutes and looks at the remainder of exhibits, it is plain that neither Stanisic nor Badza financed or supplied the VRS. The Serbian DB did not even support the RS DB. This is not to argue, and we will not argue it during our defence, that the Serbian MUP, that is the public security, did not offer assistance to the Bosnian Serbs, nor will the Defence suggest that there were not individuals with the DB who did not -- who did -- who offered ad hoc assistance to the Bosnian Serb forces. It is quite possible, for example, as alleged by Prosecution witness JF-026, that the RS MUP received aid in the form of uniforms and communication equipment from police stations in Mali Zvornik and Loznica. It was, however, a constant frustration of the Bosnian Serbs that the Serbian MUP did not provide proper assistance. Whether that submission is correct or not, the contributions offered by the Serbian MUP cannot be attributed to Mr. Stanisic. Had Mr. Stanisic been aware of any involvement of the DB resources or personnel and the training of any forces, including those that went to Bosanski Samac, he would have stopped it. We shall apply to admit the testimony of the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, Nikolic, and two men trained at that alleged Serbian DB camp, DST-68 and 57. The training was organised by the JNA commander and the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. The training lasted for only a few days and involved, it follows, only minimal resources. In other words, that and other training camps could exist without institutional support by the DB. It could exist and did exist without Mr. Stanisic's knowledge. It has nothing to do with him. These men who I've referred to, the witnesses we will apply to admit, gave evidence in the Simic trial that they were members of the RS police or the RSK police. None of them claimed any connection to Stanisic or to the mythological Red Berets. JF-047 who was recalled to this court to deal with obvious inconsistencies perjured himself for personal gain. As the Defence evidence will show, it was Mr. Stanisic's service that arrested Lugar and Debeli in Serbia when they returned from their exploits in Bosanski Samac. If Mr. Stanisic had been involved in investing so much in training these elite forces, why would he have supported their arrest upon their return to Serbia in 1992? Your Honours, I have about ten minutes. Would Your Honours allow an extra ten minutes, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're well over the two hours now. At the same time, I was informed, Mr. Groome, that there was a matter in relation to protective measures which you would like to raise; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I estimate it would take about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It might even take a bit more to the extent that I'm informed about the nature of the matter you wanted to raise. Mr. Jordash, I was asking this because we usually have a break after 75 minutes. We're now close to 70 minutes. I would suggest that we take a break first, that you then have your additional ten minutes, that we would then hear Mr. Groome --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- on the matter he would like to raise and that we finish well in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you say you have ten minutes left. Then apparently the slides are not equally -- equally distributed over the time. You are claiming that even if you would take 12 or 13 minutes, that, under the present circumstances, would not cause a great problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break. We'll resume at 12.30. Mr. Jordash, you're expected not to finish any later than 10 minutes to 1.00, and then we'll hear the further submissions by Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And so to move to a conclusion, the Defence case will show that the Prosecution interpretation of this joint criminal enterprise is but a blunt instrument. It fails to accurately define the criminal purpose, it fails to identify when it may have began with any precision, and it fails to distinguish Mr. Stanisic's actions from those actions in furtherance of a criminal purpose. The operations at Tara, the Drina operations, the operations at Pauk, and the operations in 1995 are an eloquent demonstration of that submission. The evidence will show as we've outlined that these were legitimate military operations. Of course, it was of concern and the consequences were grave, that these operations involved certain criminally disposed men. However, that does not make the essential lawfulness of the military objectives unlawful or make them part of the JCE alleged. Those who can be shown to be responsible for the sending of Arkan and those who committed crimes have a case to answer, and those who can be shown to be criminally responsible should pay the price. And the Defence will demonstrate that Mr. Stanisic had nothing to do with the choices which led to those crimes and nothing to do with the crimes. As I've indicated, the story of the Red Berets is much more straightforward. It's not even nearly as dramatic as the Prosecution witnesses and some of the documentary evidence implies. Some of the men who may have committed crimes may have been employed temporarily by the DB, but that doesn't make them forever and a day the responsibility of the DB or, particularly, of Mr. Stanisic. We rely upon the fact that Mr. Stanisic had no role in choosing and employing these reserve forces. Had he been able to micro-manage the state security in the way suggested by the Prosecution case, then he couldn't have fulfilled his essential duties. It is tempting to reach for simplistic answers and coherent stories, and the story of the Red Berets is one such tale. It is a caricature description akin to a James Bond movie with Mr. Stanisic, the caricature devil at the centre. We submit that Mr. Stanisic and the Serbian MUP has been demonised by the press, by the Serbian mythology, and lastly, now, by the Prosecution witnesses. We submit that the evidence will show that he did his best to create security within Serbia for those and all of those who were endangered by the war. That is why his service became involved in the operations towards the end of the war. We submit that it is easy to point to sections of exhibits and easy to take evidence out of context. The Defence will provide that context. If I may just refer Your Honours to slides 51 to 61 -- sorry, 56 to 61. In some ways it's a microcosm of the role Mr. Stanisic played in the Defence case we will prove. It relates to the period of the Banja Luka operations. Mr. Stanisic, in slide 56, is clearly engaged in trying to find the two pilots, French pilots, who have been taken hostage by the hot-heads from Pale. Your Honours will see on slide 56 the view of Mladic, that Jovica is looking for the pilots, and there is no doubt that he does not like Slobo. Your Honours will see from slide 57 that Stanisic is playing one of the often games he was forced to play. Bluff and double bluff is the role of an intelligence man, telling Mladic what he needed to tell in order to find the French pilots, saying he was exposed and working without the knowledge of Milosevic. And if we move further down slide 57, we see there that Mladic, presumably on information, presumably having discussed with the VRS high command, notes that a team from the Serbian DB has arrived. They are Filipovic and Bozovic. They arrived. Bozovic was a member of the reserve forces. He was forever associated with the DB from the early days. It's telling that these are the men identified as belonging to the DB. Three hundred Arkan's volunteers arrived. Mladic doesn't associate them with the DB. If Mr. Stanisic had had this long-standing arrangement and relationship with Arkan's Men, he would have known that Arkan's volunteers were part of the team from the Serbian DB. And we turn to slide 58, and can I ask, please, to just briefly for P24 -- 2545 P1 to be put on the screen. The slide 58 has Stanisic saying: "There is no command there. Political conflicts, cities are falling. Arkan is embedded there. We sent 400 people." We dispute that Arkan is embedded there is precisely the right interpretation. The right interpretation involves a meaning which effectively says that Arkan put himself there. In any event, even if Your Honours don't accept that, it is most telling that Jovica says in a list of chaos, in a list of problems, there is no command there, political conflicts, cities are falling, Arkan is there. Why does Mr. Stanisic put that in a list of problems if he personally sent him there? I mean, while Mr. Stanisic looks for the pilots. If we look over the page to slide 60, Mladic's notebook entry of the 3rd of October, 1995. Filipovic notes: "Arkan's men are operating under the control of Pecanac." And he expresses approval for that, and that's what the Prosecution rely upon. They rely upon employees of the DB, themselves forming individual relationships with the likes of Arkan and then attributing that to Mr. Stanisic. Bozovic, on slide 60, notes that: "They came with a task," referring to the Serbian MUP, "a task that they were aware of. It was agreed that the RS -- that they would replace the RS police and the RS police would go to the forward defence line. This was agreed with President Karadzic and General Milovanovic." An illustration of what our defence is, because we submit that the Banja Luka operations involved the Serbian MUP, and they involved the Serbian MUP who sent men to replace the RS police who were being dragged into the conflict, and the idea was that the Serbian MUP would replace and conduct normal security duties. That was agreed with President Karadzic and General Milovanovic. And at the bottom of slide 60 Your Honours will see a reference there to Jakovljevic: "People are openly asking who brought Arkan and under whose patronage they are doing this." 1995, it appears that no one at that time from the VRS high command associated Arkan with Stanisic. If there was a glimmer of truth in the Prosecution case, he would have been known as Arkan -- as Stanisic's man. And meanwhile, Stanisic is looking for the pilots. And then over the page to slide 61. Another demonstration of the demonisation, we suggest, which has taken place in relation to the Serbian MUP. Mladic notes he has a meeting with the inner circle of the General Staff of the VRS, and he notes that already for four days no resources have been coming from the FRY and the Serbian MUP has probably put the border under its control after Arkan was chased away. So there you have it. The Serbian MUP controlling and preventing Arkan from working. And there you have it at the bottom of slide 21 [sic], Mladic noting that they have a problem with the RS MUP after Arkan was chased away, and Tomo Kovac Minister of the Interior does not accept the order and use of the military police. In other words, there's the association: Arkan was invited by the RS MUP and prevented from returning by the Serbian MUP, and therein lies the Prosecution case exposed. And so finally, turning to Prosecution Exhibit P690, and the Prosecution put some weight on this because it -- in reality it's one of the very, very few comments from Mr. Stanisic which might be construed as indicating support for any criminal enterprise. We submit it is pre-war bravado. A proper analysis of that discussion shows that the discussion revolves around a peace agreement and the necessity for bringing people like Babic, extremists to the negotiating table, and Stanisic using inflammatory language. It is not an indication of his mens rea. It's an indication of pre-war bravado and frustration that others will not accept peace. And if we go over the page to line 63, the section missed out by the Prosecution where Stanisic says: "If they want it, they'll have an all-out war." "Yes, yes," says Karadzic. Stanisic answers: "Better do it like decent people." And in our submission, that's what the Defence will show, that Stanisic did it like a decent person, because as the witnesses will confirm, he is a decent person. And whilst cities were falling and whilst Arkan placed himself there, Stanisic was doing what he did, trying to secure Serbia by rescuing the two pilots, trying to secure that peace would come and that Serbia would not be dragged into the war, and that will be the Defence case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Just ... Mr. Bakrac and Mr. Petrovic, from yesterday's Pre-Defence Conference, the Chamber understands that you're waiving your right to make an opening statement at this stage of the proceedings. Mr. Groome has expressed some concerns about compliance with Rule 65 ter (F). I just want to emphasise that of course if you choose not to make an opening statement, that that in itself does not mean that if there are changes in the nature of the accused's Defence, then of course it would be appropriate to report that, and I take it that Mr. Groome will keep a close eye on how you will proceed during the Stanisic Defence case and the Simatovic Defence case to see whether the concern reaches levels which ask for action. Until now, it was just an expression of concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like to leave it to that at this moment. I was informed that Mr. Groome would like to raise a certain matter in relation to protective measures. Are there any other matters the parties would like to raise? Mr. Jordash, I see you are nodding no. I do not see any positive response from the Simatovic Defence. Therefore, I take it that we only have the one issue to be raised by Mr. Groome. Mr. Groome, do we need to go into private session or is there no need to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't believe there's a need, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And just so it's clear, this is unrelated to the opening that we've just heard. It's a different matter. On the 27th of September, 2010, the Defence for Jovica Stanisic sought access to all confidential inter partes materials in the case of Prosecutor v. Simic et al. The Trial Chamber granted this request on the 24th of March, 2011, with certain limitations, specifically the Trial Chamber's order required the extraction of several different categories of material, and that is the -- the title of that decision is decision on request of Jovica Stanisic for access to confidential materials in the Krajisnik and Simic et al. cases. Subsequently, the Defence for Franko Simatovic sought access to the Simic material on the 2nd of June, 2011. In the process of drafting the response to the Simatovic request, the Prosecution realised that the Simatovic Defence was previously granted access to all inter partes confidential materials in the Simic case on the 12th of April, 2005, and this was a decision rendered by the Appeals Chamber under case IT-95-9-A, entitled: "Decision on Defence Motion by Franko Simatovic for Access to Transcripts, Exhibits, Documentary Evidence, and Motions Filed by the Parties in the Simic et al. Case." The respective Defence teams of the Simic case and the Prosecution reviewed the material that the Appeals Chamber ordered to be reviewed and informed the registry that there were no issues related to protective measures or Rule 70 that needed to be resolved prior to giving the Simatovic Defence access to this material. The materials were provided on a CD to Mr. Jovanovic, then counsel for Mr. Simatovic on the 20th of July, 2005. As a matter of fairness, the Prosecution considers that both the Defence teams should have the same access to confidential materials in the Simic case. Thus the Prosecution seeks this Trial Chamber -- or requests this Trial Chamber to vary it's decision of March 2011 to -- to -- to bring that decision into conformity with the Appeals Chamber decision of the 12th of April, 2005, and to order the Prosecution to turn over the same materials that had been previously provided for the Simatovic Defence. I provided courtesy copies of the Appeals Chamber decision earlier today. If the Chamber grants this request, the Prosecution has identified no additional confidential inter partes materials subject to Rule 70, and we have located the CD that was provided the Simatovic Defence in 2005 and would be able to disclose that forthwith. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any response for any observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Only thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. Everything is as indicated by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Apart from that you were asking on the 2nd of June the same material you have received before, so if you say let's leave it to that, let the Chamber write a decision on that, is -- if that's your intention, I cannot ensure you that we will follow that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my apologies. I thought we wanted to wrap up soon. We weren't familiar with this. That's why we weren't able to locate the detail about Mr. Jovanovic and the decision dated back to 2005. So that's where the misunderstanding stemmed from. And Mr. -- the filing concerning Mr. Jovanovic dated back to 2003, and we weren't able to locate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not blaming you for having difficulties in finding the CD-ROM, although I would -- to the extent it has not been done, I would perhaps advise you to go through the list of decisions in this case so that you didn't miss one, which saves a lot of time in writing new motions which cover the same -- the same subject matter. But may I take it that what you just said is an oral withdrawal of the 2nd of June motion? Is that how we have to understand your submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I was just about to state that, but for the reasons I mentioned and the problems we had with locating late Mr. Jovanovic's material, we kindly request the OTP to hand this specific material over. That's the material we were already given back in 2005, and we withdraw our application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was provided if, Mr. Bakrac will recall, in October of 2009. He requested that we redisclose all of the material provided to Mr. Jovanovic, and this material was provided on the hard drive that the Defence was given. And if he has any trouble locating it, we will, of course, redisclose again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That then seems to be resolved. If I -- Mr. Groome will assist you in ensuring that you have this material available, whether or not it's already in your possession, whether it's once or twice in the possession of the Simatovic Defence. And you were about to say that you would withdraw the motion which is now put on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Groome and our Defence team will work together to try and locate the material, and for the record, I do withdraw our motion, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record. Then the matter itself, this Chamber -- Mr. Groome, you very much emphasised the equal position for both Defence teams. Now, I'm not going to comment on what happened in 2005. What I can do is to briefly comment on what we did in 2011. In 2011, this Chamber established that -- and in that respect referring to submissions made by the Prosecution that there are categories -- let me just have a look. That there are categories that include remuneration, provisional release, fitness to stand trial, Registry submissions of expert reports on health issues, notices of nonattendance in court, modalities of trial, protective measures, subpoenas, applications for video-conference links, as well as orders to redact the public transcript and the public broadcast of a hearing. We considered that the applicant had no forensic purpose for access. Now, the question then arises, what is more important, equality between the parties, one of the parties having received material or at least I do not know whether it existed or -- but at least not -- where access is not excluded from material which this Trial Chamber considered to have no -- no forensic purpose. Now, what to do under those circumstances, to restore equality by giving to the Stanisic Defence also material which serves no forensic purpose? There was no request for a certificate to appeal this decision in this respect. It was emphasised by the Prosecution that this did not serve any forensic purpose. Now, what is more important to restore equality by giving to the Stanisic Defence material which we consider totally without purpose to give it to them, or to say let's leave the inequality exist as it does exist and not further add to access to materials which, in the view of this Chamber, no access should have been given to at least the Appeals Chamber at that time was very much concerned about the difference between inter partes and ex parte material. Well, that's not an issue that arises here. So before the Chamber will decide, Mr. Jordash, are you interested in receiving materials without a forensic purpose just in order to restore equality in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I can probably speak on behalf of our beleaguered case manager, and the answer's no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Groome, thinking about further distribution of, I would say, material often with a -- some kind of a privacy element in it and without a forensic purpose, would you - also in view of the answer given by the Stanisic Defence - would you insist on your motion, your oral motion, that the Chamber would override the protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm not going to insist that the Stanisic Defence accept something that they do not want. I guess one of the considerations that prompted this was that I know that the two Defence teams do have some co-operation, and if one had some material that the other didn't, where we're setting up a situation where there could be an inadvertent violation of an order to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I do understand that the Defence teams, both Defence teams are so much short of time that they would certainly not discuss matters which have no forensic purpose at all. That's at least my expectation. Under the present circumstances, may I take it that the Simatovic Defence, again I do not know whether there's any provisional release material in the Simic -- you would not know either, because you don't have that material, but would you, if you receive it, would you please carefully look at whether there's any material of those categories which we listed in the decision on the Stanisic motion for access and to avoid to discuss that with the Stanisic Defence, because it is in your hands. It is confidential material. It is not accessible to the Stanisic Defence, and they have no problem with that. So if you would be very strict on that, no errors or no mistakes will occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We'll proceed as best we can, and we'll follow your guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's even another option which you could consider. The decision of the Appeals Chamber is there, and this Chamber, of course, is not in any way competent to even discuss this decision, but in view of the Chamber's decision and in view of the access granted to the Stanisic Defence, you could even invite Mr. Groome when again supplying you with the information to leave out what is not given to the Stanisic Defence and not insisting on having full disclosure of these materials. Mr. Groome, you have -- you must have two sets, the old one and the new one, the limited Stanisic one. So I leave that entirely in your hands whether you want to make such a request to the Prosecution or not. It would at least restore in practical terms the equality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, may I take it that from your earlier observation that your oral application is withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any other matter to be raised at this moment? If not, I would like to inform the parties that they will soon know whether next week Friday, which is, if I'm not mistaken, the 24th of June, that you'll be informed about whether we'll hear the evidence in the morning or the afternoon, and there is a fair chance that it would be in the afternoon, and I put you already on notice before you make any travel arrangements that there's a risk that it will be in the afternoon, but you will be informed as soon as possible. If there's no other matter, we stand adjourned, and we resume Monday -- no, Tuesday, the 21st of June, at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon in Courtroom II, I take it. Madam Registrar, could you confirm that? Yes, it is hereby confirmed. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 21st day of June, 2011, at 2.15 p.m. 22 23 24 25
